analysis.title: Ruminations - Macro, Micro, Markets (Bobby Molavi, 9 Nov 2026)
key_insights: Week of 2-6 Nov: S&P 500 fell 2.68% to 7,377, Nasdaq 3.37%, Dow 0.94%, Russell 2.05%. The path was violent: a post-election relief rally on Wednesday, an air-pocket gap lower on Thursday, then calm and some dip buying on Friday.

Thursday was the damage day: S&P -4.4%, Dow -1,833 points, Nasdaq -6.3% (worst session since the pandemic reaction), VIX up about 70%, all eleven sectors lower. Nvidia lost more than $440bn of market value in the day.

The author's primary driver was a negative reinforcing loop between performance and technicals. Losses (pnl) triggered technical stops, which forced short-duration, levered strategies to degross or liquidate. The selling hit the same reference prices that triggered the degrossing, which set off new selling ('stop bingo').

Wednesday's rally treated the Democratic sweep of both chambers as benign (gridlock is historically stock-friendly). Thursday's rout was pinned partly on fears of tighter AI and data-center regulation under the new Congress, so the election fed the AI anxiety.

The AI buildout complex led on the way down. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell over 12% on the week. Lumentum -36%, Seagate -28%, Marvell -28%, Western Digital -28%, SanDisk -27%. The author notes a further move in Nvidia on Monday on weekend 'news'.

The author's four anchors: (1) the AI debate continues, with the Democratic sweep a new factor. (2) Oil is moving lower on a GDP slowdown, no Middle East escalation, talk of talks and the Democratic win. (3) Yields are normalising as people price a possible AI capex slowdown, lower oil and the effect of the last hike. (4) Earnings are still very solid, but solid and sometimes blowout results are not enough.
H1 and Q2 were a market where everyone got paid (the author compares it to 2021). Q3 and Q4 have been too hard, with investors running just to give back much of the H1 gains.

Gross and basis became close to unmanageable last week. Spreads blew out and correlations broke in software vs semis, Apple vs Nasdaq, banks vs insurance, European banks vs European defence, defensives vs growth, small vs large cap, Europe vs US, and S&P ex-AI vs S&P.

Broadening has run for several weeks: rotation into value, small and mid cap, under-owned, defensive and real-economy names. The S&P offset big AI and tech drawdowns with staples, real estate, healthcare, consumer and travel and leisure. This reverses a market where the S&P was up 12-13% while most of its stocks were down on the year.

The author sees technicals, positioning and performance as the real story. Gross had come down but concentration had not, and AI vs SPX or Nasdaq has not worked as a hedge. Long/short has had a very hard 4 to 6 weeks and the losses spread to multi-asset, systematic, credit and convertible capital. Crowded longs suffered higher vol and big corrections while shorts also hurt as money rotated to defensives.

Crowding evidence from Goldman's PB risk team: realised 3-month alpha correlations between fundamental and systematic L/S managers were top decile of the past decade coming out of summer. Correlations between US and Asia fundamental managers hit all-time highs, driven largely by the AI trade.

Indexation and momentum argument: passive and ETF ownership, market-neutral hedge funds and systematic quant have made momentum a factor embedded in every portfolio. Over 60% of YTD returns six months into the year came from 6 stocks (35% from one). Index-tracking money never sells winners, which fuels the way up and the way down. Nvidia went from $1tn to $5.8tn and then to close to $4tn in a matter of weeks.

Bubble and terminal-value argument: past bubbles (railways, tulips, internet) permanently reshaped economies, but early capital was hurt when valuation decoupled from revenue and cash flow. Value did not always flow to the builders (Cisco and Qualcomm thrived then faltered, 360 networks, Altavista and Webvan did not survive). The question is the price of innovation and the timing of return, not its value.

Circularity in AI is unusually high, citing the Nvidia and OpenAI deal, Nvidia's stake in Intel, Oracle and Nvidia GPUs, and hyperscalers holding stakes in AI startups. The author describes 2026 as a mega-FOMO trade in which fear of missing AI capex outweighed the risk of spending too early or too much.

Valuation: forward P/E troughs were 10.4x (March 2009), 13.3x (March 2020) and 15.7x (October 2022). If last week was a trough, the S&P settled at 18x, which the author calls cheaper rather than cheap. He notes this ignores growth rates.

Charts flagged: Vol Panic Index had its biggest 2-day round trip on record. Semis are down about 28% in one month, one of the largest rolling 1-month drawdowns in history. A key support level was touched and held so far. The S&P staples valuation premium to SPX is the highest in 10+ years. QQQ set a notional volume record of $86bn, which the author uses to separate volume from liquidity. Momentum, the leading factor, is faltering.
Friday gave some pause. The author says next week determines whether it was a momentary bounce or a new floor to build from.

sector_views.rationale: The author reports the group led the unwind, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down over 12% on the week and about 28% over one month. He gives no formal rating.

Staples outperformed in the rotation. The report flags their valuation premium to the S&P at a 10+ year high and a forward multiple about 2x the semiconductor index's, which raises the question of what is now overbought.

earnings_insights: Earnings are described as still very solid, and in some cases blowout, but the report says that is not enough to support prices in the current tape. No company figures are given.
risk_factors: Another round of forced degrossing if Friday's bounce fails and concentrated AI longs keep falling.
Further AI capex slowdown pricing and possible AI and data-center regulation under the new Congress.
Circular financing and interdependence among AI firms, so stress at one name can spread to the others.
Crowding and correlation across fundamental and systematic managers mean AI, which was not an effective hedge, can drive losses everywhere at once.
Staples now trade at a 10+ year premium to the S&P, so the defensive rotation itself may be crowded.
Growth rates are the missing part of the valuation argument, so 18x forward P/E may not be a trough.

tension_points.bull_case: If last week was the trough, the S&P settled at 18x forward P/E, above the 10.4x, 13.3x and 15.7x troughs of 2009, 2020 and 2022. The author calls this cheaper rather than cheap, and notes a key support level was touched and held, with Friday showing some bottom dipping.
tension_points.bear_case: The troughs cited do not factor in growth rates, which the author calls an essential and missing part of the mix. Staples trade at a 10+ year premium to the S&P and the S&P is still concentrated, so crowding and forced selling can return.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The author says next week is key on whether Friday's bounce was momentary or a new floor. A failure of Friday's bounce would invalidate the floor view.

tension_points.bull_case: Past bubbles left lasting infrastructure and value (railways, internet), and the rush to innovate created the bedrock for later waves. Dominant stakes in AI infrastructure could pay off, and earnings remain very solid.
tension_points.bear_case: Value does not always flow to the builders (Cisco, Qualcomm, 360 networks, Altavista, Webvan). AI is unusually circular, and early capital was hurt when valuation decoupled from revenue and cash flow. The AI complex is leading the market down, with semis down about 28% in a month.
